newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.N. Rwanda genocide court told of torture.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda genocide court told of torture.

text.p: A Hutu peasant farmer testifying before the U.N. Rwanda genocide tribunal stripped off his shirt on Tuesday to show scars he said were sustained when he was tortured and beaten by a former government official.

The former government official, Jean-Paul Akayesu, is in the dock charged with genocide and crimes against humanity during the mass slaughter of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994.
The witness, a coffee farmer and the second one since the trial reopened last week, was only identified as "Witness C" in order to protect his identity.

Witness C said Akayesu, a former mayor of Rwanda's central Taba commune, spent a night terrorising him because of his refusal to reveal the whereabouts of a Tutsi woman, named only as Alexia, whom he had hidden at home.
Akayesu has pleaded not guilty. If convicted he will face life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty.
Trials have also opened in the Rwandan capital Kigali of a suspected ringleader of the genocide, Froduald Karamira, and four other defendants.

Karamira, a former businessman and politician, is the most prominent suspect to go on trial. He was arrested in Addis Ababa in June and extradited to Rwanda where he faces death penalty by firing squad if convicted.

In three hours of horrific testimony, Witness C described how Akayesu and extremist Interahamwe Hutu militiamen put him in a car and drove him to a forest near Taba commune in the middle of the night.
There he was made to lie on his back in front of the car and Akayesu stamped on his face and nose bursting his lips while the militiamen beat him with rifle butts, he said.
Later he was interrogated, beaten again, tied by the neck to another woman being tortured so that he vomited and forced to strike her with a cudgel.
"My body is no longer what it was before. My nose bleeds and I have pains in my head" since that night, the witness said.
Despite his efforts to protect Alexia, she was found. She was taken to Akayesu's office the next morning and killed, the witness said.
He said he tried to shelter her because she was a friend and he did not want to get involved with killings.
He also said he attended a meeting during the genocide at which Akayesu incited citizens to view Tutsis as the enemy, though he was unable to give the meeting's date.
Rwanda is a country ethnically torn between minority Tutsis, who now control its national army, and majority Hutus, driven out of power after the three-month genocide.
Presiding Judge Laity Kama gave Akayesu permission to look at the witness's wounds at close range and he stepped from behind his glass screen towering over the shirtless farmer.
The testimony adds a fresh dimension to earlier evidence by suggesting Akayesu physically partipated in atrocities.
The session was adjourned until Wednesday when Kama said Akayesu would have the chance to cross-examine Witness C.

Earlier "Witness K", a Rwandan Tutsi accountant in Akayesu's office, told the court she witnessed Akayesu order eight Tutsis hacked to death on April 19, 1994. Akayesu cross-examined her on Monday and Tuesday but she stood firm on her central claim.

Akayesu is the first suspect to be tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda set up to bring to justice the architects of the genocide sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president Juvenal Habyarimana in April 1994.
Angry Hutu followers, militiamen and soldiers took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to Habyarimana's junta.
